nameStory: Green-keeled cottongrass gets its name from the fluffy white seed heads that look exactly like tufts of cotton dancing in the wind. The 'green-keeled' part refers to the green ridge running down the back of each leaf blade, like the keel of a boat cutting through water.
description: Green-keeled cottongrass is a graceful wetland sedge that produces stunning white, cotton-like seed heads in summer. This slender plant grows 1-3 feet tall in clumps, with narrow grass-like leaves and stems topped by fluffy white plumes. Despite its name, it's not actually a grass but a sedge - you can tell because its stems are triangular rather than round. The cottony seed heads make it one of the most recognizable and beautiful plants in New England's wetlands.

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Fluffy white cotton-ball clusters at stem tips in summer, each tuft made of thousands of silky bristles that catch and shimmer in the breeze

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Triangular stems that feel distinctly three-sided when rolled between your fingers - this sedge family trait separates it from true grasses

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves with a prominent green ridge (keel) running down the center that you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose clumps or colonies, typically 1-3 feet tall, often growing in patches across wet meadows and bog edges

idTips.label: Early Flowers
idTips.description: Before the cotton stage, produces small brownish flower spikes that look unremarkable compared to the showy seed heads that follow

habitat: Look for green-keeled cottongrass in wet, acidic soils of bogs, fens, wet meadows, and marshy areas throughout New England. It thrives in permanently moist to saturated soils and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. You'll often find it growing alongside other bog plants like cranberries, pitcher plants, and sphagnum moss.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from wet soil, looking like thin grass blades with that distinctive keeled ridge becoming visible as leaves mature.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time when the spectacular white cottony seed heads appear, creating drifts of white across wetlands from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads gradually disperse in the wind, leaving bare triangular stems, while leaves may turn golden-brown before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving little trace except perhaps some persistent dried stems in protected spots.

funFact: Each cottony seed head contains up to 200,000 individual seeds, and the fluffy bristles can carry seeds over 60 miles on a windy day - making cottongrass one of nature's most efficient long-distance colonizers!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its cousin tawny cottongrass, but tawny has rusty-brown seed heads while green-keeled produces pure white cotton. Remember: green-keeled = white cotton, tawny = brownish cotton. The keeled leaf ridge is also more pronounced in green-keeled cottongrass.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - cottongrass isn't a grass at all, but a sedge. The confusion comes from the grass-like leaves, but the triangular stems and cotton-ball seed heads are dead giveaways that this plant belongs to the sedge family. Historically, people used the cottony seed heads as pillow stuffing and lamp wicks.
compareHints: Among New England's cottongrasses, green-keeled stands out with its bright white seed heads and prominently ridged leaves. Tawny cottongrass has brownish seed heads, while tussock cottongrass forms distinctive large clumps and has multiple cotton heads per stem. Common cottongrass typically has several drooping seed heads per stem, unlike green-keeled's usually single upright cotton tuft.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's cottongrasses, tawny cottongrass is unique for its brown seed heads - common cottongrass and tussock cottongrass both have white or cream-colored fluff.
Tussock cottongrass is the only cottongrass that grows in distinctive single tussocks and produces just one seed head per stem.
Rough cottongrass is the smallest and most delicate of New England's cottongrasses.
Common cottongrass typically has multiple nodding seed heads per stem, while tussock cottongrass usually has just one erect cottony head per stem.
Among New England's cottongrasses, slender cottongrass stands out for its thin, delicate build and preference for the wettest bog conditions.
